12. It is pertinent to point out that a negotiable instrument carries following presumptions in terms of Section 118 (a) and 139 of NI Act.

(a) Section 118 of the NI Act provides : "Presumptions as to negotiable instruments:
Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made:
of consideration that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has been accepted, indorsed,
negotiated or transferred was accepted, indorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration;"
Section 139 of the N.I Act further provides as follows: "Presumption in favour of holder it shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in Section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability".
13. The combined effect of the presumptions under Section 118 (a) and Section 139 has been dealt by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in a catena of judgments.
The principles pertaining to presumptions and onus of proof were summarized by Hon'ble SC in Basalingappa vs Mudibasappa, (2019) 5 SCC 418 .

sentences.text: We having noticed the ratio laid down by this Court in the above cases on Sections 118(a) and 139, we now summarise the principles enumerated by this Court in following manner.
25.1. Once the execution of cheque is admitted Section 139 of the Act mandates a presumption that the cheque was for the discharge of any debt or other liability.
25.2. The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise the probable defence.
The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities.

25.3. To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or the accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence.
Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely.
25.4. That it is not necessary for the witness to come in the witness in support of his defence.
Section 139 imposed an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden.
25.5. It is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box to support his defence."

14. Further, recently in Tedhi Singh v. Narayan Dass Mahant Cr. Appeal No. 362 of 2022, the Hon'ble Apex Court held:
"It is true that this is a case under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act.

entities.text: Tedhi Singh v. Narayan Dass Mahant Cr. Appeal No. 362 of 2022

sentences.text:
Section 139 of the N.I. Act provides that Court shall presume that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in Section 138 for the discharge,
in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability.
This presumption, however, is expressly made subject to the position being proved to the contrary.
In other words, it is open to the accused to establish that there is no consideration received.
It is in the context of this provision that the theory of 'probable defence' has grown.
In an earlier judgment, in fact, which has also been adverted to in Basalingappa (supra), this Court notes that Section 139 of the N.I. Act is an example of reverse onus [see (2010) 11 SCC 441).
It is also true that this Court has found that the accused is not expected to discharge an unduly high standard of proof.
It is accordingly that the principle has developed that all which the accused needs to establish is a probable defence.
As to whether a probable defence has been established is a matter to be decided on the facts of each case on the conspectus of evidence and circumstances that exist."

15. Thus, it is clear that once the execution of cheque is admitted by or proved by the complainant,
the presumptions under Section 118 (a) and 139 of NI Act have to be compulsorily raised including that the same was for discharge of any existing debt or liability and thereafter, onus shifts on the accused to raise a probable defence.

sentences.text: Bearing the principles in mind, I proceed to evaluate whether the ingredients of the offence under Section 138 are satisfied.
Notably, there is no dispute at bar with respect to the proof of only first, third and fourth ingredient.
It is not in dispute that the cheques in question were drawn by the accused from his bank account and were presented within its validity period.
Further, it is also not in dispute that the accused is the signatory of the cheques in question as in the notice framed under Section 251 CrPC, he has duly admitted the same.
Presentation of the cheques in question by the complainant is also not in dispute.

The dishonour of cheque in question by way of return memos Ex.
CW1/3 is also not in dispute, hence it is clear that it was returned for reasons "Funds Insufficient".
17.
The complainant sent the legal demand notice dated 26.11.2018 Ex. CW1/4 (Colly), at the addresses of the accused, by way of India post.
The same was received by the accused on 01.12.2018 as evinced from tracking report.
However, the accused has denied receiving the legal notice in his examination u/s 313 CrPC though he has admitted receiving the same at the time of framing of notice u/s 251 CrPC.

Be that as it may, pertinent is that the processes of the court has been served on the same address of accused mentioned in the memo of parties and the same address mentioned in the memo of parties is also mentioned in the legal notice served upon the accused.

Moreover,
accused has furnished the same address as mentioned in the legal notice as well as memo of parties in his Form 45/personal bond furnished by him.
Significantly, the accused has also admitted in his cross-examination that he resides at the address mentioned in the memo of parties and the legal notice.
Thus, it is pertinent to point out that it is not case of the accused that legal demand notice was sent on an incorrect address, rather, the accused has stated that the same was not received by him.

The Hon'ble Apex Court in CC Alavi Hazi v. Palapetty Muhammad & Anr. (2007) 6 SCC 555 has held that:
" Any drawer who claims that he did not receive any notice by post, can, within 15 days of the receipt of summons from the court in respect of the complaint under section 138 NI Act, make payment of the cheque amount and submit to the court that he had made the payment within 15 days of receipt of summons (by receiving a copy of complaint with summons) and therefore, the complaint is liable to be rejected.

sentences.text: A person who does not pay within 15 days of the receipt of summons from the court along with the copy of the complaint under section 138 of NI Act, cannot obviously contend that there was no proper service of notice as required U/s 138 of NI Act, by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary under Section 27 of General Clauses Act and Section 114 of Evidence Act."
18. Thus, in view of the above discussion, the demand legal notice is held to have been duly served upon the accused.
As such the first, third, fourth and fifth ingredient of the offence under section 138 NI Act have been duly satisfied.
Further, as noted above, accused has admitted his signatures on cheques in question and hence a presumption under Section 139 of NI Act has to be raised in favour of the complainant.
19. Regarding the second ingredient of the offence, there is a dispute between the parties.
In view of the same, the onus of proof shifts upon the accused to rebut the presumption that such liability does not exist.

Hence, it is now to be examined as to whether the accused has brought any material on M/S Ved Prakash Ashish Kumar vs . R.K Trading Company on 22 May, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/190260331/

sentences.text: It is trite that for this purpose accused can rely on his own evidence or can also rely upon the materials submitted by the complainant to raise a probable defence.

In the matter at hand, the accused has taken the defence in his application under Section 145 (2) NI Act that the cheque in question was given as a security cheque that has been misused by the complainant.
20. In the context of the defence of accused, the evidence of the parties may be examined.
During the cross-examination, CW1 denied the suggestion that there is no partnership firm with the name of Ved Prakash Ashish Kumar.
He further denied that he does not have any right or authority to issue bills in the absence of registration of partnership firm.
He further deposed that the cheque amount is the balance amount of the total bill amount.
He further denied the suggestion that the bills Ex. CW1/1 (Colly) are forged and fabricated and therefore he has not filed certificate u/s 65 B Evidence Act.
He further denied the suggestion that the cheque in question was a security cheque issued for previous transactions which has been misused by him.
The witness admitted that the particulars in the cheque in question have been filled by him and only the signatures are in the handwriting of the accused.
The witness further explained in his deposition that the particulars in the cheque were filled on the instructions of the accused.
CW1 further admitted that there was no purchase order placed from the side of accused but explained that the purchase orders are usually placed verbally.
He denied that the accused has no liability towards the cheque in question and towards his firm.
CW1 hi further evidence (when application u/s Section 311 was allowed) has tendered the partnership deed dated 1.04.2003 Ex. CW1/6 on record.
In his further cross-examination, he denied the suggestion that partnership deed is forged and fabricated.
21. DW1 in his examination-in-chief deposed that he is engaged in the business of sugar and the complainant used to supply sugar bags to him.
He further deposed that the cheque in question was given as a security in blank signed condition.
He further stated that only a liability of Rs. 50,000/- is remaining upon him and the complainant has misused the cheque in question.

He further stated that he used to give orders on his leter pad for supply of sugar and according to his knowledge the complainant firm has been closed.

In his cross-examination, DW1 admitted that he know Mr. Ashish Kumar as he used to purchase goods from him.
He further admitted that he had received the goods from the complainant firm.
He further stated that he did not receive the invoices Ex. CW1/1 (Colly).
In response to the question of Ld. Counsel for complainant of making the payment of Rs. 2 lacs on 14.03.2018 and Rs. 1 lac on 24.07.2018, DW1 admitted that he had made the payment.
However, he further testified that he does not remember if he had made any payment through bank transfer thereafter.
DW1 further admitted that he does not have any receipt of the cash payment made to the complainant.
He further testified that he does not remember when and how much cash payment he had made to the complainant.
He denied that he had given the cheque in question on account of liability towards the complainant.

sentences.text: It is also important to point out that the accused in his cross-examination has also admitted that he used to purchase goods from the complainant's firm.

The Hon'ble Kerala High Court in Abdul Gafoor v. Abdurahiman (1999) 4 Crimes 98 has held that effect of non-registration of the Partnership Firm under Section 69 of the Partnership Act is applicable only to cases involving civil rights and it has no application to criminal cases.
Under the provisions of Partnership Act, all partners are agents of the Partnership Firm and therefore, every partner is competent to represent the firm and to give evidence on behalf of the firm.
Similar view has been taken by Hon'ble Supreme Court in BSI Ltd. & Anr. V. Gift Holdings Pvt. Ltd. (2000) SCC (Cri) 538.

sentences.text: Therefore, the contention of the accused that the prosecution under Section 138 NI Act is not sustainable cannot be accepted.
24. The next objection is with regard to non-submission of Certificate u/s 65 B Evidence Act and mentioning of 24 % interest in the legal notice on the cheque amount.
It is not is dispute that the accused in his statement u/s 313 CrPC has admitted the bills Ex. CW1/1 and the liability thereon.
The legal notice also clearly specifies the amount that is due on the part of the accused.
Thus, the superficial defences raised by the accused do not find favour of this court and therefore stands rejected.
25. It further emerges that the accused has also taken the objection that the cheque in question was given as a security and the particulars of the same were not filled by him.

In this context, it is necessary to take note of the judgment of Hon'ble Delhi High Court in Ravi Chopra v. State & Anr.
(2008) 102 DRJ 147, wherein the Hon'ble Court held:
"20.

sentences.text: A collective reading of the above said provisions shows that even under the scheme of the NI Act it is possible for the drawer of a cheque to give a blank cheque signed by him to the payee and consent either impliedly or expressly to the said cheque being filled up at a subsequent point in time and presented for payment by the drawee.

There is no provision in the NI Act which either defines the difference in handwriting or the ink pertaining to the material particulars filled up in comparison with the signatures thereon as constituting a 'material alteration' for the purposes of Section 87 NI Act.
What however is essential is that the cheque must have been signed by the drawer.
If the signature is altered or does not tally with the normal signature of the maker, that would be a material alteration.

Therefore, as long as the cheque has been signed by the drawer, the fact that the ink in which the name and figures are written or the date is filled up is different from the ink of the signature in not a material alteration for the purposes of Section 87 NI Act."
26. It is an admitted position that the cheque in question has been signed by the accused as he has admitted the same during the framing of notice u/s 251 CrPC.
The complainant in his cross-examination has disclosed that the particulars in the cheque were filled by him at the instructions of the accused.

For the reasons explained in the judgment cited above, it matters little if the other particulars in the cheque in question have been filled up at a subsequent point in time and by whom i.e. the complainant or accused as the same would not constitute any 'material alteration'
for the purposes of Section 87 of NI Act.

In other words, merely because the particulars in cheque in M/S Ved Prakash Ashish Kumar vs . R.K Trading Company on 22 May, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/190260331/
8 question have not been filled by the accused, that by itself will not go to prove that the accused has discharged the liability towards the complainant.

27. The next objection taken by the accused is with the regard to the cheque in question was issued as a security cheque for the previous transactions.
In this context, it would be apposite to refer to the observations of the Hon'ble Delhi High Court in Suresh Chand Goyal v. Amit Singhal Crl.

Appeal No.
601/2015 decided on 14.05.2015:

"28. There is no magic in the word "security cheque", such that, the moment the accused claims that the dishonoured cheque (in respect whereof a complaint under Section 138 of the Act is preferred)
was given as a "security cheque", the Magistrate would acquit the accused.
The expression "security cheque" is not a statutorily defined expression in the NI Act.
The NI Act does not per se carve out an exception in respect of a "security cheque" to say that a complaint in respect of such a cheque would not be maintainable.

There can be mirade situations in which the cheque issued by the accused may be called as security cheque, or may have been issued by way of a security, i.e. to provide an assurance or comfort to the drawee, that in case of failure of the primary consideration on the due date, or on the happening (or not happening) of a contingency, the security may be enforced.
While in some situations, the dishonor of such a cheque may attract the penal provisions contained in Section 138 of the Act, in others it may not."

28. Similarly, in Credential Leasing & Credits Ltd. v. Shruti Investments & Anr. (2015) 223 DLT 343,
the Hon'ble Delhi High Court interalia, held as follows:
"30.

sentences.text: Thus, I am of the considered view that there is no merit in the legal submission of the respondent accused that only on account of the fact that the cheque in question was issued as security in respect of a contingent liability, the complaint under Section 138 of the NI Act would not be maintainable.

At the same time, I may add that it would need examination on a case to case basis as to whether, on the date of presentation of the dishonoured cheque the ascertained and crystallised debt or other liability did not exist.

The onus to raise a probable defence would lie on the accused,
as the law raises a presumption in favour of the holder of the cheque that the dishonoured cheque was issued in respect of a debt or other liability.

As settled by the Supreme Court, the said onus obliges the accused to raise a defence - either by picking holes in the case of the complainant and/ or by positively leading defence evidence which leads the Court to believe that there is a probable defence raised by the accused to the claim of the complainant with regard to the existence of the debt or other liability.

The said onus does not cast as stringent an obligation on the accused,
as it casts on the complainant, who has to prove beyond reasonable doubt the guilt of the accused."
29.

In this regard, it is for the defence to raise a probable defence to cast a doubt on the claim of the complainant with regard to the existence of an ascertained and crystallised debt or other liability in relation to the transaction in respect whereof the cheque in question has been asserted to have been M/S Ved Prakash Ashish Kumar vs . sentences.text: Coming to the facts of the present case, CW1 has produced the bills Ex. CW1/1 (Colly) on record to substantiate his claim.
He has further deposed that the cheque amount is the balance amount out of the total bill amount.
Importantly, the accused in his statement u/s 313 CrPC has admitted that "There is some liability on my part that I have to discharge in favour of the complainant.
I used to take goods from the complainant.
There is some remaining amount that I have to pay on the bills Ex. CW1/1 (Colly) to the complainant".

The defence set up the accused that the cheque was a security cheque for previous transactions is unbelievable and merely an ipsi dixit as the accused has admitted the bills Ex. CW1/1 (Colly), the receipt of goods under the same and payment of some amount pending upon them.
Thus, the debt/liability of the accused to the tune of the cheque amount stood ascertained, crystallised and established from his statement u/s 313 CrPC.
Consequently, the defence that the cheque in question was issued as a security for previous transactions deserves to be rejected.
30. The next defence of the accused is that that only a sum of Rs. 50,000/- is remaining to be payable on his part and not the cheque amount.
Significantly, the accused has neither disclosed this stand in his application u/s 145 (2) NI Act nor gave any suggestion on this aspect to the complainant during his cross-examination.
Be that as it may, accused during his cross-examination/evidence has failed to bring on record any document to show as to how and when the cash amount has been paid to the complainant.

It is noteworthy that the reason for dishonour of cheques is "Insufficient funds"
and the accused has not bothered, neither to give any instructions to his bank to stop the payment qua the cheque in question nor filed any complaint with the police or gave any notice to the complainant.
It is inconceivable to a reasonable mind that a person whose cheques have been misused will not give instructions to his bank to stop payment as soon as he discovers the same.
This again raises a suspicion over the claim of the accused that the only a sum of Rs. 50,000 is remaining to be payable and the complainant has misused the cheque in question.
Thus, the defence of the accused qua remaining amount of only Rs. 50,000/- does not inspire confidence and is baseless and vague.

31. In view of the foregoing discussion, I am of the opinion that the present complainant has disclosed the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability vide the cheque in question, return memo and legal notice brought on record.
The complainant has successfully proved all the necessary ingredients of Section 138 NI Act and the accused has failed to rebut the presumption by raising any probable defence.
Hence, accused Jagdish Prasad S/o Lt. Ram Kumar, Prop. of RK Trading Company stands convicted of the offence punishable under Section 138 of NI Act.
